question: What is the main goal of positioning a patient correctly in bed?

options.A: Maintaining body alignment and preventing complications
options.B: Reducing the cost of hospital stay
options.C: Eliminating the need for daily bed baths

explanation: You're doing great! Keeping a patient in proper alignment protects their joints and stops pressure sores before they start. It's a simple step that makes a huge difference. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h1)

question: Why should a midwife carefully plan when and how to change a patient's position?

options.A: To follow a strict hospital cleaning schedule
options.B: To reduce the number of required nursing staff
options.C: To ensure the patient stays asleep all night
options.D: To meet individual comfort and clinical safety needs

explanation: Every mum and patient is unique. Planning their position changes keeps them comfortable and safe based on what their body needs right now. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h1)

question: Which position means the patient is lying flat on their back?
explanation: Think 'supine = spine on the bed'. It simply means lying flat on the back with the face pointing up. You've got this! [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h2)

question: A patient in the ward is struggling to catch their breath. Which position helps them breathe easier right away?
explanation: Raising the head of the bed into Fowler's position lets the chest expand fully. It's a quick, natural way to give a breathless patient some relief. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h2)

question: What actually happens to the skin and body during a shear injury?

options.A: Skin rubs directly against rough clothing material
options.B: Blood pressure drops suddenly due to rapid movement
options.C: Joints become locked in a fixed position
options.D: Underlying bone moves while skin stays fixed to the sheet

explanation: Shear happens when a patient slides down in bed—the skeleton moves, but friction holds the outer skin stuck to the sheets. This stretches and tears tiny blood vessels underneath! [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h3)

question: How can you best protect a patient's skin from friction when moving them up in bed?

options.A: Using a draw sheet to lift the patient slightly off the mattress
options.B: Pulling the patient quickly by their ankles across the sheets
options.C: Asking the patient to slide down using their bare heels
options.D: Applying heavy lotion to the bedsheets before moving the patient

explanation: Always lift, don't drag! Using a draw sheet clears the mattress surface so you avoid rubbing their skin raw. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h3)

question: To prevent pressure sores, how often should an immobile patient be turned and repositioned?
explanation: The golden rule for pressure care is every 2 hours! This gives tiny blood vessels a chance to get blood flow back before skin damage sets in. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h4)

question: Your patient is resting comfortably on their side (lateral position). Which bony spot is at the highest risk for pressure damage?
explanation: When lying on the side, all that body weight rests right on the side of the hip—the greater trochanter. Be sure to check and pad that area! [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h4)

question: Why is lying flat on her back dangerous for a woman in late pregnancy?

options.A: It stops the placenta from receiving oxygen from the air
options.B: It compresses the inferior vena cava, reducing blood return to the heart
options.C: It causes the diaphragm to move too high into the chest
options.D: It immediately triggers active labor contractions

explanation: In advanced pregnancy, the heavy womb presses heavily on the main blood vessel (inferior vena cava) when flat on the back, causing dizziness and low blood pressure. Always prop her up or turn her to the side! [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h5)

question: What is the main physical benefit of helping a patient sit upright in bed?

options.B: Complete prevention of deep vein thrombosis
options.C: Decreased blood flow to the lower extremities
options.D: Improved lung expansion and easier breathing

explanation: Gravity is our helper here! Sitting up lets the diaphragm drop down, making it much easier for the lungs to fill with air. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h5)

question: When lifting a heavy patient, which part of your body should do most of the work to protect your back?
explanation: Protect your back! Always bend your knees and use your powerful leg and thigh muscles to lift, keeping your spine safe and straight. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h6)

question: Why do nurses and midwives count out loud ("1, 2, 3, lift!") when moving a patient together?

options.A: To ensure everyone lifts at the exact same moment for safety
options.B: To comply with hospital administrative regulations
options.C: To signal visitors to leave the room during the transfer
options.D: To keep the patient awake and aware of the procedure

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! Counting together ensures every team member applies force at the exact same second, keeping both staff and the patient safe. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h6)

question: What essential details must you write in the patient's chart right after repositioning them?

options.A: Patient's favorite sleeping position at home
options.B: Time, specific position used, and skin condition
options.C: Cost of the pillows and wedges used
options.D: Name of the hospital furniture manufacturer

explanation: Good charting proves good care was given. Always note the exact time, the position you used, and what the skin looked like. [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a good reason for documenting patient positioning?

options.A: Protecting the nurse and hospital against legal negligence claims
options.B: Tracking the prevention of pressure injuries over time
options.C: Giving nursing staff an excuse to avoid checking on patients
options.D: Providing a clear record for the healthcare team

explanation: Documentation is there to communicate care and protect patient safety—never as an excuse to skip checking on your patients! [learn more](BMP110_U4_T8#BMP110_U4_T8_h7)
